The present claim petition arises out of road accident in which one minor, master Abhishek Kumar, aged about 7 years, sustained grievous injury resulting in permanent disability.
An application u/s 166 (1) MV Act was accordingly filed by the claimant through his legal guardian.

2. Brief facts of the case are that on 25.01.2018, at about 5:30 -06:00 p.m., master Abhishek along with one Gautam Kumar (aged about 15 years), were returning from tuition classes on motorcycle bearing no.UP16-BF-3076, which was driven by one Neeraj.

When their motorcycle reached Havert Company crossing, a speeding truck bearing no.RJ-01GA-9045 (hereinafter referred to as the offending vehicle), hit the motorcycle causing Abhishek vs Gopal Singh Rawat on 12 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149378006/

Separate claim petitions were filed seeking compensation qua death of victim Gautam Kumar and the present one, seeking compensation qua injury resulting in disability caused to victim Gautam Kumar.

Issue No.1
Whether this Tribunal has territorial jurisdiction to entertained this petition?OPP 12.
In the present case, jurisdiction of this Tribunal has been claimed on the basis of location of one of the branch offices of respondent no.2 within the territorial jurisdiction of this Tribunal.
As per law settled in Malti Sardar vs. NIC, there is no bar to a claim petition being filed at a place where the insurance company, which is the main contesting party, has its business.
Thus, the plea of lack of Territorial Jurisdiction is unsustainable and issue is accordingly decided.

Contributory negligence 17.

The insurance company has raised a defence of contributory negligence on the part of the victims on the ground that they were triple riding on a motorcycle without wearing helmets and that the driver of the motorcycle was also without a driving licence.

The fact of triple riding is not in controversy however, it is only when such triple riding contributed to the occurrence of the accident,
would it amount to contributory negligence.
There is nothing in the FIR or the chargesheet or the evidence led by the petitioners to show that the accident occurred due to disbalancing of the motorcycle on account of triple riding.
The insurance company has failed to establish any nexus between the occurrence of the accident and the triple riding by the victims.

In the peculiar facts of the case, it is evident and undenied that the victims, though triple riding on the motorcycle and though not wearing helmets, were driving on the correct side of the road and it was the offending vehicle that came from the opposite direction breaching the traffic signal.
Respondent no.1 MACT no.768/2018 Abhishek & anr. vs. Gopal Singh Rawat & ors. Page no. 8 of 23 ss has neither cross examined PW-2 nor led any evidence to prove the contrary.

Reliance is placed upon decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sudheer Kumar Rana vs. Surinder Singh (2008) 12 SCC 436, which held as under:-
"9.

sentences.text: If a person drives a vehicle without a licence, he commits an offence.
The same, by itself, in our opinion, may not lead to a finding of negligence as regards the accident.
It has been held by the courts below that it was the driver of the mini truck who was driving rashly and negligently.
It is one thing to say that the appellant was not possessing any licence but no finding of fact has been arrived at that he was driving the two-wheeler rashly and negligently.

If he was not driving rashly and negligently which contributed to the accident, we fail to see as to how, only because he was not having a licence, he would be held to be guilty of contributory negligence."

Similar view was taken in Mohd. Siddiqui vs. National Insurance company Ltd. AIR 2020 SC 520 wherein it was held that a pillion rider, even if accompanied by more than the legally permitted numbers of passengers, does not automatically imply contributory negligence.

sentences.text: The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

sentences.text: ......In the case of Susamma Thomas (supra), this Court issued certain guidelines in order to "safeguard the feed from being frittered away by the beneficiaries due to ignorance, illiteracy and susceptibility to exploitation".

Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of MACT no.768/2018 Abhishek & anr. vs. Gopal Singh Rawat & ors. Page no. 19 of 23 ss minors, illiterate claimants and widows.

sentences.text: In the case of illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living.
However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to withdraw money.

In the case of semi-illiterate claimants,
the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid.
In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos.
(i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should.

Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit MACT no.768/2018 Abhishek & anr. vs. Gopal Singh Rawat & ors. Page no. 20 of 23 ss and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons.

sentences.text: However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit.

They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semiliterate and literate persons.

It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds.
The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money.

The fact of triple riding is not in controversy however, it is only when such triple riding contributed to the occurrence of the accident,
would it amount to contributory negligence.
There is nothing in the FIR or the chargesheet or the evidence led by the petitioners to show that the accident occurred due to disbalancing of the motorcycle on account of triple riding.
The insurance company has failed to establish any nexus between the occurrence of the accident and the triple riding by the victims.
In the peculiar facts of the case, it is evident and undenied that the victims, though triple riding on the motorcycle and though not wearing helmets, were driving on the correct side of the road and it was the offending vehicle that came from the opposite direction breaching the traffic signal.

There is nothing in the facts to suggest that the accident occurred because of motorcycle being driven in violation of traffic law for not having a driving licence or because the victim was triple riding or because none of them were wearing helmet.
